title: Discontinuity of the phase transition for the planar random-cluster and Potts models with q > 4 (Theorems 1.1 and 1.2)

abstract: Formalizes Gregory Morse and Tamas Kozsik's paper "Tamper-Proofing with Self-Modifying Code" (arXiv:2604.12407v1). The selected statement (PalomarSMT.mathematical_result, four results T1-T4) is an abstract threat model for checksum units whose opcode state lives in the memory they checksum: a system of units with regions and code, a timeline of write, execute, check, split-view and DMA events, adversary levels L0-L4, a cost contract with lower bounds on emulation, forgery and mediation, and eight structural assumptions A1-A8 (none of the form "the attacker is detected"). An effective alarm needs a unit with a response code (at least one response byte, all of it unmodified) and either a value mismatch or a positive number k of consecutive timing failures; A6 therefore includes k > 0 and A7 includes that every unit has a response byte. The four selected results are: for every well-formed timeline of a system satisfying A1-A8, if a protected byte outside the SMC opcode bytes (which legitimately vary) is executed while the fetch view differs from the original image, an effective alarm occurs somewhere in the timeline, not necessarily before that execution (T1; executing a changed protected opcode byte is outside the goal); in a faithful split-view run every iteration with a non-zero toggle (apart from the last) is mediated, and under A3 and A5 a faithful mediated check that the cost contract admits, with such an iteration, is a timing failure (T2; not every split-view attack is claimed detected); each of the eleven assumptions is necessary, by an explicit winning adversary against a system that satisfies all the others (T3); and every well-formed timeline at level L0 or L1 with the inline timer satisfies A1, A4 and A5, while there are winning adversaries against systems satisfying every other assumption at L1 with an operating-system timer, at L2 and at L4 (T4: the removed assumption is A5 at L1 with an operating-system timer and at L2, A1 at L2, A4 at L4). Proved in the same development but NOT part of this record (they are not in the Comparator configuration): the paper's Harvard/von Neumann observation (C01, C02), a general fact about observation-preserving simulation whose time bound assumes the per-read charge it uses; the three-quadword forgery of the checksum and the proof that two quadwords do not suffice (the selected T3 witness for A8 is a single two-quadword collision pair); the x86-64 model of the kernels, the static kernel against its C emulation, the 296-unit unrolled kernel at an abstract level and at the instruction level, the byte layout against assembler output, a clear-count contract checked against the paper's tables, timers, the noise estimator, the detection predicate and the data ratios, and native test vectors for the corrected sources.
title: Tamper-proofing with self-modifying code: threat model, security and necessity of the assumptions

abstract:
A Lean formalization of a technical lemma in the paper "Nonlinear lower-tail large deviations at criticality" by Matthew Kwan and Huy Tuan Pham. This lemma is used to solve a certain variational problem, which is necessary to characterise the probability that a random graph is triangle-free in the so-called "critical regime" where the edge probability is of order 1 / sqrt n.
Specifically, this lemma defines a "certificate function" G and proves that it satisfies a certain inequality. This involves lots of interval arithmetic.
title: A certificate for the triangle variational problem

abstract: A Lean 4 development of Kuhn's simplified two-person poker (Kuhn 1950): three cards 1 < 2 < 3, one dealt to each player with the six deals equiprobable, an ante of a from each player and a single bet of b, player I acting first, the five courses of play of Kuhn's p. 98 with payoffs a (pass-pass, to the higher card), a to II (pass-bet-pass), a + b to the higher card (pass-bet-bet), a to I (bet-pass) and a + b to the higher card (bet-bet). The definitions are built from the game tree: a behaviour strategy of I is a pair of functions on the three cards (the probability of betting first, the probability of calling after passing and facing a bet), one of II likewise (the probability of betting after a pass, the probability of calling a bet); the payoff is the average over the six deals; a strategy guarantees v when it is valid and earns at least v (holds the opponent to at most v) against every valid strategy of the opponent; the game has value v when each player has a strategy guaranteeing v; an equilibrium is a saddle point. For Kuhn's game a = b = 1, kernel-checked: the value is -1/18 (a game has at most one value), an equilibrium exists, every equilibrium pays I exactly -1/18, and a pair is an equilibrium iff each strategy guarantees -1/18; II's optimal strategy is unique at all six information sets (bet after a pass with the 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 1/3, 0, 1; call with probabilities 0, 1/3, 1 - Kuhn's (xi, eta) = (1/3, 1/3) with the four coordinates he removed as superfluous now proved forced); I's optimal strategies are exactly Kuhn's one-parameter family (bet the 1 with probability alpha and fold it, never bet the 2 first and call with it with probability alpha + 1/3, bet the 3 with probability 3 alpha and call with it, for alpha in [0, 1/3], the call with the 3 being unconstrained exactly when 3 alpha = 1, where that information set is unreached); in the normal form with Kuhn's coding of the 27 and 64 pure strategies, his essential 8 x 4 matrix is six times the game matrix, his twelve basic optimal mixed strategies (A)-(L) and II's two guarantee -1/18, and a mixed strategy is optimal iff its realization plan lies on the family (I) or its marginals are II's strategy (II). For every ante a > 0 and bet b > 0 (Kuhn's pp. 102-103, stated there without proof, and the region b > 2a he does not state): the value is -b^2/(6(2a + b)) for b <= a, -b(2a - b)/(6(2a + b)) for a <= b <= 2a and 0 for b >= 2a, with explicit guaranteeing strategies in each case; in Case 3 the calling probability eta with the 2 ranges over [(2a - b)/(2a + b), b/(2a + b)], and the interval printed on p. 102, b/(2a + b) <= eta <= (a + b)/(2a + b), fails at its upper end (at a = 2, b = 3 and eta = 5/7 II's Case 3 strategy does not guarantee the value). Every guarantee is a finite nonnegative-product identity (the gap between the payoff and the value is a sum of products of the opponent's probabilities and their complements with coefficients nonnegative on the case's region: polynomials in a, b and the free parameter, at general stakes built from a, b, 2a + b, a - b, 2a - b, 4a - b, b - 2a and the interval factors (2a + b)eta - (2a - b), b - (2a + b)eta, 2(a - b) - (2a + b)xi, and, in the optimal-set theorems, the slacks of their stated inequalities), and every "only if" is a linear certificate from finitely many pure strategies (the coefficients rationals at a = b = 1 and, at general stakes, polynomials in a, b and the free parameter nonnegative on the case's region); no formal library found by the dated search holds the game. Beyond Kuhn's statements: the two certificate identities are stated as theorems; the equilibria of Kuhn's game are exactly the pairs (kuhnI α k, kuhnII) with α in [0, 1/3], k in [0, 1] and 3α = 1 or k = 1; and at general stakes the optimal sets are determined - I's strategy is unique for b < a (up to the unreached call with the 3) and for a < b <= 2a, is Kuhn's family on the diagonal b = a at every scale, and for b >= 2a never bets the 1 or the 2 first, folds them, and with the 3 is cut out by one inequality (a single strategy at b = 2a; beyond it a two-dimensional set in which I may also bet the 3 first, with probability at most (b - 2a)/b), so Kuhn's one-parameter family is optimal only at b = a; II's strategy is unique on the diagonal at every scale and a segment for b <= a (the bet with the 2 after a pass free in [0, 2(a - b)/(2a + b)], so Kuhn's 'unique optimal mode of behavior' in Case 1 holds in his behaviour parameters only); for a <= b < 2a its bets after a pass are forced, (b/(2a + b), 0, 1), and its calls form a polytope of three inequalities; for b > 2a it never bets the 1 or the 2 after a pass, never calls with them, and calls with the 3 with probability at least 4a/(2a + b), its bet with the 3 free; and on the line b = 2a its optimal set is a five-dimensional polytope (the bet with the 2 after a pass zero and, with bets (p, 0, r) and calls (s, t, w), 2p <= r, s + t <= p, 1 <= t + w, 1 + p + s <= 2w; nine vertices, replayed); at every ante a > 0 and bet b > 0 every equilibrium pays the value and a pair is an equilibrium iff each strategy guarantees it, so the equilibria are exactly the pairs of optimal strategies, on b = 2a explicitly; the corrected Case 3 interval is sharp, and the printed one holds only at its lower end. A second correction, a misprint, is noted in the documentation: p. 101's table gives β = 5/12 for (I) and (J), where p. 100's mixtures and p. 101's own formula give 7/12.
title: Kuhn poker: the value −1/18, all optimal strategies, and the solution at every ante and bet

abstract: A Lean 4 development of Graham's two bounds for scheduling independent jobs on identical machines to minimize the makespan (R. L. Graham, Bounds for certain multiprocessing anomalies, Bell System Tech. J. 45 (1966) 1563-1581; Bounds on multiprocessing timing anomalies, SIAM J. Appl. Math. 17 (1969) 416-429; both restated with their examples in his survey Bounds on multiprocessing anomalies and related packing algorithms, AFIPS Spring Joint Computer Conference (1972) 205-217). n jobs of nonnegative real lengths p : Fin n -> R are run without interruption on m >= 1 identical machines; an assignment sigma : Fin n -> Fin m loads machine i with the sum of the lengths assigned to it, its makespan is the largest load, and optMakespan m p is the least makespan over all m^n assignments. A list schedule (IsListSchedule, in the index order) gives each job a machine whose load from the earlier jobs is least, under any tie-breaking (a relation, so every theorem covers every tie-breaking); an LPT schedule (IsLPTSchedule) is a list schedule of the jobs in some nonincreasing order of length. Theorems, kernel-only: every list schedule sigma and every assignment tau satisfy m * C(sigma) <= (2m - 1) * C(tau) (Graham 1966, his Theorem for the same number of processors and no precedence constraints), so C(sigma) <= (2 - 1/m) * optMakespan; the m(m - 1) unit jobs followed by one job of length m (Graham's example for his theorem on scheduling the k largest tasks optimally first, at k = 0, as his 1972 survey restates it; Lenstra-Shmoys, Chapter 9, p. 188) have optimum m and every list schedule of them in that order has makespan 2m - 1, so 2 - 1/m is the least constant (IsLeast); every LPT schedule sigma and every assignment tau satisfy 3m * C(sigma) <= (4m - 1) * C(tau) (Graham 1969, Theorem 2, announced in the closing remarks of the 1966 paper), so C(sigma) <= (4/3 - 1/(3m)) * optMakespan; when every job is longer than a third of C(tau), every LPT schedule is at least as good as tau, so LPT is optimal when every job exceeds a third of the optimum; Graham's 2m + 1 jobs 2m - 1, 2m - 1, 2m - 2, 2m - 2, ..., m + 1, m + 1, m, m, m (his pp. 425-426) are in nonincreasing order, have optimum 3m, attained by a list schedule in the order 2m - 1, ..., m + 1, m, m, 2m - 1, ..., m + 1, m (the definition grahamOrder, a permutation of the jobs whose lengths are that list), and every LPT schedule of them has makespan 4m - 1, for every m >= 1, so 4/3 - 1/(3m) is the least constant (IsLeast); and the elementary facts (list and LPT schedules exist, the optimum is attained, every load, every job and the average load are at most the makespan, relabeling the jobs preserves the makespan); Graham's omega_0, the least finishing time over all lists, equals the optimum over all assignments (every assignment is matched or improved by a list schedule in some order), so the bounds against every assignment are his; for his instance the optimum is attained by an explicit list (grahamOrder); and the third of the optimality theorem cannot be weakened (on three machines 9, 5, 5, 4, 4, 4, each job at least a third of the optimum 12, has an LPT schedule of makespan 13, so n <= 2m jobs do not make LPT optimal; Graham's 1972 survey prints Spencer's 6, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2 for the same purpose); and the position of a job on its machine: the (c + 1)-th job k placed on a machine of a list schedule of a nonincreasing p has (c + 1) p_k <= C(tau) for every assignment tau (the property of Chen 1993, as Della Croce-Scatamacchia 2020 restate it; proved here by an invariant on pairs of machines), hence the Coffman-Sethi form q m C(sigma) <= ((q + 1) m - 1) C(tau) for a machine with q jobs attaining the makespan of an LPT schedule (Coffman-Sethi 1976 as corrected by Chen 1993, as Della Croce-Scatamacchia restate it; the literature states it for q >= 3, for m >= 2 it is weaker than the 4/3 - 1/(3m) bound at q <= 2, and neither its attainment nor Chen's 4/3 - 1/(3(m - 1)) at q = 2 is proved here; Chen's and Coffman-Sethi's papers were not read). The proof of the LPT bound is by counting, not by his exchange argument: with k the job ending a heaviest machine, the average-load bound settles 3 p_k <= C(tau), and otherwise a count of the jobs up to k (every machine of tau holds at most two of them, those at least as long as the least load sit alone, each single-job machine of sigma contributes one) shows that k's machine ends by C(tau). Further: for a job k completing at the makespan of a list schedule of a nonincreasing p, the smaller of C(sigma) and 3 p_k is at most C(tau) for every tau, and C(sigma) <= 3 p_k certifies optimality; equality 3m C(sigma) = (4m - 1) C(tau) on m >= 2 machines forces 3 p_k = C(tau), equal loads before k, every load of tau equal to C(tau) and no positive job after k; Della Croce-Scatamacchia's Proposition 4, q (m - 1) C(sigma) <= ((q + 1)(m - 1) - 1) C(tau) when another machine holds q jobs before k and q + 2 <= m, proved from Chen's property; Dósa's theorem (2004, Theorem 2: Graham's example is the only tight one): every positive multiple of Graham's 2m + 1 jobs in any order attains the bound, and for a nonempty positive instance on m >= 2 machines a list schedule in nonincreasing order, or an LPT schedule in any order, attains 3m C(sigma) = (4m - 1) optMakespan only when the instance is a positive multiple of Graham's jobs, so the inequality is strict for every number of jobs other than 2m + 1; and for every fixed n >= 2m + 1 the constant 4/3 - 1/(3m) is the supremum (IsLUB) of C(sigma)/optMakespan over the LPT schedules of the positive instances with n jobs (the proof approaches it with Graham's jobs followed by small jobs; Dósa's Remark 1 asserts a strict gap for every n != 2m + 1, which can therefore hold at most for n < 2m + 1, not formalized here). Forty-one compared statements over nine fully specified definitions; the finite facts behind every statement are replayed exactly in the standard library by scripts/check_lpt.py. As of 2026-10-11 no kernel-checked proof of the 4/3 - 1/(3m) bound, of either equality family or of the optimality statement was located in the Palomar registry, Mathlib, formal-conjectures, openai/math, anthropics/formal-math, the Isabelle AFP, the Rocq package index, GitHub code search in Lean or arXiv; the AFP's Approximation_Algorithms proves a 3/2 bound for sorted greedy and the factor 2 for greedy, and two Lean repositories prove m * C <= sum p + (m - 1) * p_max over lists of naturals. No priority is claimed.
title: Graham's bounds for list scheduling and LPT on identical machines: 2 − 1/m, 4/3 − 1/(3m) and their tight instances

abstract: Five compared theorems. Among all substitutions on at most three letters whose incidence matrix has a Pisot eigenvalue θ > 1, the least such θ is the plastic number ρ, the real root of x³ = x + 1, attained only by the Padovan rule a ↦ b, b ↦ c, c ↦ ab and its mirror c ↦ ba, up to renaming the letters; both minimal rules are chiral, in opposite directions. Precisely: (1) for a substitution σ on k ≤ 3 letters (images may be empty) and a real eigenvalue θ > 1 of its integer incidence matrix that is a Pisot number, ρ ≤ θ, and θ = ρ exactly when, after renaming the letters, σ is the Padovan rule or its mirror; no primitivity or unit hypothesis; (2) the same classification for every real eigenvalue, with no Pisot hypothesis; (3) a 3 × 3 natural matrix with characteristic polynomial x³ − x − 1 is the Padovan matrix after one simultaneous permutation of rows and columns; (4) Siegel's bound ρ ≤ θ for Pisot numbers of degree at most three (Siegel 1944, restricted; not new; proved through the minimal Mahler measures of registered entry PALOMAR-2026-08-31-000004); (5) under the Padovan rule the word ca is a factor of the fifth iterate from the seed a, and ac is a factor of no iterate from any seed; under its mirror, the reverse. The uniqueness was stated without proof by Mercat (2020) for substitutions on three letters; the contribution is a kernel-checked proof of the combined statement, for every real eigenvalue and with no primitivity, unit or non-erasing hypothesis (in the equality case these are consequences: θ = ρ forces k = 3 and characteristic polynomial x³ − x − 1), together with the chirality of both minimal rules. No first-formalization claim is made. That ρ itself is a Pisot eigenvalue of the Padovan matrix, so that the bound is attained, is proved in Supplement.lean and not compared. Companion of registered entry PALOMAR-2026-08-19-000006.
title: The Arithmetic of Time: the slowest settling clock on at most three letters is the Padovan substitution, unique up to mirror image, and both minimal rules are chiral

abstract: Kernel-checked proof, for every Coxeter system on three generators a, b, c with m(a,c) = p, m(b,c) = q, m(a,b) = infinity and p, q >= 2, of the growth-series identity in the ring of integer power series: (sum_n a(n) X^n) * (1 - (X + ... + X^(p-1))(X + ... + X^(q-1))) = (1 + X)(1 + ... + X^(p-1))(1 + ... + X^(q-1)), where a(n) is the number of group elements of Coxeter length n; together with its instances (2,3,inf), (2,4,inf), (3,3,inf) and, for (2,3,inf) = PGL(2,Z), the sphere sizes 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 12, 16, ..., the Padovan identity a(n) = Pad(n+5) for n >= 2, the two-sided bounds 2 rho^n <= a(n) <= 4 rho^n (n >= 2), and the growth rate a(n)^(1/n) -> rho, the plastic number, the unique real root > 1 of x^3 = x + 1; and, for the whole family, monotonicity and symmetry in (p, q), the growth rate of every hyperbolic member, and the minimality of the plastic number. Twenty compared theorems: (1) the general identity for all p, q >= 2; (2) non-vacuity, a Coxeter matrix of that type exists for all p, q >= 2; (3)-(5) the three instances; (6) the (2,3,inf) sphere sizes a(0..4) = 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and the recursion a(n+5) = a(n+3) + a(n+2) for all n; (7) that the recursion fails one step earlier, a(4) != a(2) + a(1); (8) a(n) = Pad(n+5) for n >= 2, for any sequence with the Padovan initial values and recursion; (9) existence and uniqueness of the plastic number; (10) the bounds; (11) the n-th-root limit; (12) monotonicity: a(n) of a (p,q,inf) system is at most a(n) of a (p',q',inf) system for p <= p', q <= q'; (13) symmetry in p and q; (14) 2 rho^n <= a(n), n >= 2, for every hyperbolic member; (15) for (p,q) != (2,2) exactly one tau > 1 solves (tau^-1 + ... + tau^-(p-1))(tau^-1 + ... + tau^-(q-1)) = 1; (16) a(n)^(1/n) -> tau; (17) tau strictly increasing in (p,q); (18) rho <= tau with equality exactly at (2,3), (3,2), so the plastic number is the minimal growth rate of the family; (19) tau < 2; (20) tau -> 2 as p, q -> infinity (for every sigma < 2 there is N with tau > sigma whenever p, q >= N). The family statements (12)-(20) give the growth rate of every hyperbolic (p, q, inf) group as the unique root tau > 1 of an explicit equation, strictly increasing in the labels, with the plastic number as the family minimum attained only at (2,3,inf) and (3,2,inf); they restrict to this family, and kernel-check there, Terragni's monotonicity (2016, Thm. A), Floyd's planar minimality (1992, p. 482) and the continuity of the growth rate (Floyd 1992; Yukita 2024). The mathematics is classical and no novelty is claimed for it: the growth series of a Coxeter group is rational and determined by its finite parabolic subgroups (Steinberg 1968; Humphreys 1990 Section 5.12); growth of planar hyperbolic Coxeter groups is Floyd 1992 and Cannon-Wagreich 1992, and the (2,3,inf), (2,4,inf) and (3,3,inf) sphere sequences are OEIS A096231, A179070 (shifted) and A054886, with generating functions derived there from Cannon-Wagreich Prop. 3.1 and, for A096231, the Padovan form a(n) = A000931(n+10) recorded; Floyd 1992 (p. 482) proves (2,3,inf) minimal among cusped planar groups and Kellerhals 2013 gives an alternative proof; Bucher-Talambutsa 2016 Prop. 18 proves statement (11) itself by a normal form and, with Mann's bound, the minimality of rho for PGL(2,Z) over all generating sets. The (p, q, inf) family is hyperbolic exactly when (p, q) differs from (2, 2); the affine (2, 2, inf) is included in (1). The contribution claimed is the kernel-checked general identity for all p, q at once, and the family statements (12)-(20) derived from it, from Mathlib's CoxeterSystem alone — Mathlib at this pin has no growth series, no exchange or deletion property and no parabolic-subgroup API — by constructing the amalgam normal forms, lifting their action to the group, proving Coxeter length equals normal-form length, and counting. No "first formalization" claim is made. Application, cited and not a claim of the entry: the (2,3,inf) group is the Weyl group of AE_3 = PGL(2,Z) (Feingold-Frenkel 1983) and, in the Damour-Henneaux-Nicolai billiard description of the Belinski-Khalatnikov-Lifshitz limit (a conjecture for generic singularities, Henneaux-Persson-Spindel 2008 Section 2.9), the reflection group of the billiard of 3+1-dimensional vacuum gravity near a spacelike singularity (Damour-Henneaux-Nicolai 2003 Section 8; Henneaux-Persson-Spindel 2008 Section 3.1), where a(n) counts the chambers reachable from the fundamental chamber after exactly n wall collisions over all initial data, so (10)-(11) give the growth rate of those outcomes (elementary reflection-group geometry, not formal content). Hypotheses are inline: the Coxeter system enters through Mathlib's CoxeterSystem with the three matrix entries as hypotheses, rho through its defining equation and 1 < rho, the Padovan sequence through its initial values and recursion; the compared statements use only core Mathlib vocabulary (CoxeterMatrix, CoxeterSystem, CoxeterSystem.length, Nat.card, PowerSeries.mk, Finset.range/Ico sums, Filter.Tendsto, Filter.atTop, nhds, real powers) — zero custom definitions. The pinned source of each Coxeter-specific imported definition, and of Nat.card and PowerSeries.mk, is quoted verbatim, with permalinks, in MATHLIB_DEFINITIONS.md (the remaining vocabulary is standard Mathlib and is not quoted), and DefinitionAudit.lean kernel-checks the facts the statements rely on (the entry 0 encodes infinity; length is the minimal word length; spheres are finite and Nat.card is their cardinality; every Coxeter matrix has a Coxeter system).
title: Growth series of the triangle Coxeter groups (p, q, infinity), with the PGL(2,Z) instance: Padovan sphere sizes and growth rate the plastic number

abstract: Kernel-checked certificates for the multiplicative compositum of the two registered Mahler minimizers — rho, the real root of x^3 = x + 1 (the plastic number: Smyth's nonreciprocal minimum, Siegel's smallest Pisot number) and Q, the real root > 1 of x^4 = x + 1 (the degree-4 entry of the minimal-measure tables) — together with the Bedford-Kim spectral family whose limit rho is, and (new in version 2) the identification of that family with the Coxeter-element spectra of the E_m star trees. Twenty-two compared theorems. The spectral half: (1) for n >= 7 the family chi_n(x) = x^(n+1)(x^3 - x - 1) + (x^3 + x^2 - 1) has a canonical root in [117/100, rho), largest below rho, strictly increasing, tending to rho; (2) every chi_n is strictly positive on [rho, infinity); (3) chi_7 = (x - 1) * L exactly, over any commutative ring, with L Lehmer's degree-10 polynomial; (4) L has a root in [117/100, rho). The compositum half, for the degree-12 minimal polynomial of rho * Q (written out in full in every compared statement): (5) an exclusion witness — a nonreal quartic root z with 1 < |rho * z| < rho * Q; (6) the twelve embedding products ARE the conjugates of rho * Q, both directions; (7) there are exactly twelve of them; (8) rho * Q is an algebraic unit, via an explicit degree-11 cofactor over any commutative ring — the (3, 4, 12) triple in the normal form alpha * beta * gamma = 1; (9) the degree-12 polynomial is not reciprocal (neither its reversal nor the reversal's negation), placing it in the regime of Smyth's theorem; (10) degree multiplicativity — deg minpoly(rho*Q) = deg minpoly(rho) * deg minpoly(Q) = 12; (11) the compositum in sup form Q(rho) join Q(Q) = Q(rho*Q), of degree 12, with the two simple extensions linearly disjoint; (12) the complete unit-circle census — EXACTLY 5 conjugates strictly outside, EXACTLY 7 strictly inside, NONE on the circle, so rho * Q is neither a Pisot nor a Salem number; (13) the house — every conjugate other than rho * Q has modulus strictly below rho * Q; (14) the exact Mahler measure M = rho^2 * Q^2 * psi, where psi is the real root > 1 of psi^4 = psi^3 + 1; (15) the registry bridge — M(X^4 - X - 1) = psi and M(rulerPoly) = (rho * Q)^2 * M(X^4 - X - 1), re-proving in-repo the quantity pinned in registered entry PALOMAR-2026-08-31-000004; (16) the order-12 Hadamard product recurrence — the termwise product of any solutions of the cubic and quartic shift recurrences satisfies the order-12 recurrence whose characteristic polynomial is exactly the degree-12 polynomial, in any Q-algebra; (17) the annihilator ideal of the product power sequence n |-> (rho * Q)^n is EXACTLY the principal ideal of the degree-12 polynomial — the classical order <= 3 * 4 bound is an equality, forced by the polynomial's kernel-held irreducibility. THE COXETER BRIDGE (version 2), for the star trees E_m = T(2,3,m-3) with generalized Cartan matrix A given entrywise and Coxeter element c = s_0 s_1 ... s_{m-1}, each simple reflection the matrix s_i = 1 - e_i e_i^T A of the geometric representation: (18) for every m >= 4, (X - 1) * charpoly(c) = X^(m-2)(X^3 - X - 1) + (X^3 + X^2 - 1) — the classical E_n Coxeter-polynomial identity (recorded in Gross-Hironaka-McMullen 2009, Section 1, and proved there as Cor. 4.3 for n >= 4), whose right-hand side is chi_{m-3}: the spectral half of this entry IS the E_m Coxeter spectrum; (19) with the E_10 Cartan matrix written out, the Coxeter polynomial of E_10 is Lehmer's polynomial; (20) for every m >= 10 the Coxeter polynomial of E_m has a root lambda_m in [117/100, rho) with no real root above it, the lambda_m strictly increasing and tending to rho; (21) for every m >= 10 the complexified Coxeter element has an eigenvalue lambda in (1, rho) and every complex eigenvalue is unimodular, lambda, or 1/lambda; (22) that lambda dominates the modulus of every eigenvalue and is a Salem number, for every m >= 10, with the Salem predicate written out as in the registered entry PALOMAR-2026-09-02-000003. Two disclosures of version 1 are discharged by (21)-(22) for n >= 7: the Salem property of the Bedford-Kim roots is now kernel-held, and the interval (1, 117/100) is now swept (the only eigenvalues off the unit circle are lambda_m and its inverse). The results address four research audiences: the degree problem for products and composita of algebraic numbers (the certified (3,4,12) witness at a canonically distinguished pair, in the field's own unit-product normal form); the Mahler-measure tradition (the measure of the composed product of the two degree-minimal polynomials, in closed form in the second-smallest Pisot number); composed products of polynomials (a certified rational instance where the finite-field coprimality criterion is unavailable and irreducibility is proved by elimination); and, new, Coxeter groups and Salem numbers (McMullen; Gross-Hironaka-McMullen; Hironaka's Lehmer program): the E_m Coxeter spectra, their Salem radii and their limit rho as one kernel-checked family — with the Lean audience served by concrete exercise of the Mahler-measure, linear-disjointness, Matrix.charpoly and spectrum APIs. Like the golden ratio, rho * Q is an algebraic unit of norm -1; the compared cofactor identity is that norm computation, certified. No novelty claim is made for the measure identity (the entry is not aware of it in the literature; the claimed contribution is the kernel certificate), none for the mathematics of (18)-(22), which is classical (the claimed contribution is the kernel-checked bridge from the registered Bedford-Kim family to the E_m Coxeter elements, for every m >= 4 (bridge) and every m >= 10 (spectrum, Salem) at once), no "first formalization" claim is made anywhere, and whether rho is ATTAINED as a dynamical degree is open in the literature — no statement claims it. Hypotheses are inline: rho, Q, psi enter only through their defining equations plus root-selection inequalities, the E_m Cartan matrices only through their entries, and the compared statements use only core Mathlib vocabulary (Filter.Tendsto, nhds, the complex norm, minpoly, Polynomial.rootSet, Set.ncard, Polynomial.mahlerMeasure, IntermediateField adjoin/sup, Module.finrank, Finset.range sums, Matrix.charpoly, Matrix.diagonal, List.finRange/List.prod, matrix literals, Matrix.map, spectrum, IsIntegral, Polynomial.aeval) — zero custom definitions. The name prefix "ruler" in statement names is the source project's term for the product rho * Q; nothing in any statement depends on it.
title: The compositum of the two Mahler minimizers: exact measure, conjugate census, house, and minimal product recurrence, with the Bedford-Kim plastic family, Lehmer's polynomial, and the E_m Coxeter bridge

abstract: On a fixed flat Lorentz frame with metric diag(1,1,1,-1), sources are symmetric 4x4 tensor-valued functions of the six real components of an antisymmetric field. Twelve kernel-checked statements. Among all symmetric homogeneous quadratic sources (210 free coefficients), the six infinitesimal Lorentz covariance equations together with zero trace select the Maxwell stress (the electromagnetic energy-momentum tensor) up to a unique real scale, and a displayed certificate of 209 linear coefficient equations is equivalent to both laws. Among the same homogeneous quadratic sources, conservation alone - vanishing divergence on every source-free Maxwell/Bianchi first jet - selects the same line, with covariance, trace zero and Hodge invariance derived rather than assumed. The globally C^3 symmetric conserved sources are exactly an explicit seventeen-parameter family (constant, a six-parameter cross term, and the stress), and with covariance zero field value is equivalent to zero trace and to the stress line. Under the sourceful exchange law at current stiffness k (the real factor multiplying the jet current), every everywhere-differentiable symmetric source is a constant plus the Maxwell stress of scale exactly k, and conversely, with no polynomial, degree, C^3, covariance or trace hypothesis; zero field value selects the stress. Explicit counterexamples show that covariance and zero trace are each necessary in the quadratic selection, and that covariance and the zero-field normalization are each necessary in the C^3 selection. Uniqueness of the Maxwell stress tensor is classical (Fock 1964; Kerrighan 1982; Navarro-Sancho 2012; the classification of Maxwell conservation laws by Anco-Pohjanpelto 2001); the contribution is the constructive, kernel-checked development on the explicit register at finite regularity, with finite certificates, the covariance-free routes, and the differentiable-only sourceful statement. Pisot Dimensional Theory motivates the frame; no physical coupling is selected.
title: Selection of the electromagnetic source tensor by covariance, conservation and the exchange law

abstract: A Lean 4 development of Section 3 of Lagarias, Mallows and Wilks, Beyond the Descartes circle theorem (Amer. Math. Monthly 109 (2002) 338-361), in the Lorentz form. An oriented sphere in R^n with centre x and signed radius r has the augmented curvature-centre row (|x|^2/r - r, 1/r, x/r); an oriented hyperplane <h, y> = delta with unit normal h has the row (2 delta, 0, h) (LMW Definition 3.2, (3.7)-(3.9)). Tangency is distance-encoded in LMW's oriented sense: two spheres dist^2 = (r + s)^2 (external tangency for two positive radii, internal when one radius is negative), a sphere and a hyperplane <h, x> - delta = -r, two hyperplanes opposite unit normals, LMW's oriented tangency pair by pair, and the converses deliver tangency in this sense; the compatible orientations of an oriented Descartes configuration (disjoint interiors, with the given orientations or all reversed) are proved separately for every solution, after multiplying each row's power polynomial by the total curvature, and for a valid, pairwise tangent family with positive total curvature for its own open interiors. Kernel-checked, for every n >= 1 (LMW's Section 3 assumes n >= 2; their Section 8, (8.4), is the identity on the line): the augmented matrix W of n + 2 pairwise tangent spheres of nonzero curvature, and of n + 2 pairwise tangent spheres and hyperplanes, satisfies W^T Q_n W = [[0, -4, 0], [-4, 0, 0], [0, 0, 2 I_n]] with Q_n = I - (1/n) 11^T (Theorem 3.3); every real solution W is the augmented matrix of exactly one family of valid, pairwise tangent oriented spheres and hyperplanes, and, when its second column has no zero, of exactly one pairwise tangent family of spheres (the converse of Theorem 3.3); the Soddy-Gosset relation (sum 1/r_i)^2 = n sum (1/r_i)^2 with and without hyperplanes (Theorem 1.2, (1.2)) and its form b^T Q_n b = 0 ((3.2)); the curvature-centre identity M^T Q_n M = diag(0, 2 I_n) (Theorem 3.2, (3.5)); at n = 2 the complex Descartes theorem (sum b_i z_i)^2 = 2 sum (b_i z_i)^2 and sum b_i (b_i z_i) = (1/2)(sum b_i)(sum b_i z_i) (Theorem 2.1, (2.2)-(2.3)); det Q_n = -2/n; and the three statements for Mathlib's EuclideanGeometry.Sphere (pairwise IsExtTangent, or one enclosing sphere to which the others are IsIntTangent, with curvature -1/r_e). The matrix identity is proved as LMW's Section 4 argument (Lemmas 4.3-4.4, (4.9)-(4.10)) run directly in Euclidean coordinates: W^T Q_n W is the target exactly when the rows of W have Lorentz norm 1 and pair to -1 under G = [[0, -1/2, 0], [-1/2, 0, 0], [0, 0, I_n]], since W G W^T = 2I - J and (2I - J)(Q_n/2) = I. Also proved: both halves of the converse of the Soddy-Gosset theorem, LMW's Theorem 3.1, about which they write "We do not know an easy proof of this result; a proof appears in [16]" ([16] is Graham-Lagarias-Mallows-Wilks-Yan III, whose arXiv versions 1-2 prove both halves as their Theorem 2.2 from the same base configuration and the transitivity of the Lorentz group, a section the published version omits). Existence: every nonzero b with (sum b_i)^2 = n sum b_i^2 is the curvature vector of a pairwise tangent family of spheres, where b_i is nonzero, and hyperplanes, where b_i = 0, and of a family of spheres when no b_i vanishes, by one Q_n-reflection from the configuration of two parallel hyperplanes and n unit spheres in the proof of GLMWY III's Theorem 6.1, or from its inversion in the unit sphere. Congruence: two valid, pairwise tangent families with the same curvatures, index by index, are carried one to the other by exactly one Euclidean motion x -> x O + t with O^T O = I, reflections and hyperplanes included, with O = (1/2) X^T Q_n X' and t = -(1/4) a^T Q_n X' for augmented matrices [a | b | X] and [a' | b | X'] and the motion's action on points, spheres and hyperplanes; W_1^-1 W_2 preserves the target form and fixes the curvature coordinate, and every such matrix is a motion matrix (GLMWY III's arXiv v1-v2 argue instead by the rigidity of a simplex of centres); its uniqueness and parameters are proved here. A motion preserves validity, curvature and tangency, so two valid, pairwise tangent families are congruent exactly when their curvature vectors agree. For every solution W: the total curvature B is nonzero, the open sets {y : B F_i(y) < 0}, F_i(y) = b_i |y|^2 - 2 <v_i, y> + a_i the power polynomial of row i (negative exactly inside a ball, outside a ball of negative radius, or on the side of a hyperplane its normal points to), are pairwise disjoint, at most two rows are hyperplanes, and no three boundaries pass through a finite point; for a valid, pairwise tangent family the total curvature is nonzero, at most two members are hyperplanes, and when the total curvature is positive the open interiors are pairwise disjoint. The converse of Theorem 3.2 in every dimension under the hypothesis of a nonzero first column (every real M with M^T Q_n M = diag(0, 2 I_n) and a nonzero first column is the curvature-centre matrix of exactly one family of valid, pairwise tangent oriented spheres and hyperplanes), which GLMWY I, Theorem 3.1 and its Remark, prove at n = 2 with that hypothesis and which LMW's printed converse ("any real solution M") and GLMWY III's arXiv v1-v2 Theorem 2.3 omit, together with the matrix at n = 2 with columns 0, e_0 - e_1, e_2 - e_3 (GLMWY I's configuration (3.15) with its first column zeroed; the matrix of four oriented lines with normals +-e_0, +-e_1), which solves the equation and is the curvature-centre matrix of no valid, pairwise tangent family. The existence of a configuration in every dimension (that configuration); for n >= 2 the Apollonian generators S_k = I + (2/(n-1)) e_k 1^T - (2n/(n-1)) e_k e_k^T of GLMWY III, (4.1), preserve Q_n and carry configurations to configurations, with the row formula (S_k W)_k = (2/(n-1)) sum_{i != k} W_i - W_k, and Soddy's two spheres (LMW, footnote 3; GLMWY III, Section 4.1), in the signed sense: the oriented spheres and hyperplanes tangent to n + 1 members of a configuration are exactly the missing member and its Apollonian reflection, two distinct objects whose curvatures sum to (2/(n-1)) times the sum of the others' curvatures. The planar Soddy-Gosset relation for four circles of positive radius, pairwise externally tangent or with one enclosing circle, is already in Lean in facebookresearch/atlas-lean (descartes_circle_theorem, not registered); rjwalters/lean-genius and carlok/LeanFrontier treat the planar relation as a definition (its two roots, the same over the complex numbers, integer reflections and parity; LeanFrontier checks it for one family of Ford circles and their tangent line), with no derivation from tangency; no other formalization of these statements was found by the dated searches.
title: The augmented Descartes theorem in every dimension, its converses, and Soddy's two spheres

abstract: A Lean 4 development of two structures of finite-dimensional quantum information, in the vocabulary of google-deepmind/formal-conjectures (Open Quantum Problems 13 and 23; the fourteen definitions restated character for character under their Apache-2.0 license, see NOTICE). A basis of C^d is a unitary matrix whose columns are the basis vectors; two bases U, V are mutually unbiased when every entry of U^* V has squared norm 1/d; HasMUBs d k says k pairwise unbiased bases exist and IsMaxMUBCount d k that k is the largest such number. Theorems: for d >= 2, HasMUBs d m implies m <= d + 1 (Wootters-Fields 1989; Bandyopadhyay-Boykin-Roychowdhury-Vatan 2002, Theorem 3.5: the identity and the m(d - 1) traceless combinations of the rank-one projectors are pairwise orthogonal in the d^2-dimensional matrix space), and the hypothesis is sharp since in dimension 1 every two bases are unbiased; restriction to subfamilies; the tensor bound HasMUBs m k and HasMUBs n k imply HasMUBs (m n) k (Klappenecker-Rötteler 2004, Lemma 3) and its corollary over the factorization (HasMUBs d k whenever k <= q + 1 for every exact prime-power divisor q of d), hence three mutually unbiased bases in every dimension d >= 2; for a finite field F of odd characteristic and size q, the standard basis and the q bases with entries psi(a x^2 + b x)/sqrt q (psi a nontrivial additive character) are q + 1 mutually unbiased bases (Klappenecker-Rötteler, Theorem 2), through the identity |sum_x psi(c x^2 + e x)|^2 = q for c != 0 proved by Weyl differencing; for q = 2^n the bases with entries i^(x^T S_a x) (-1)^(b . x)/sqrt q, S_a the {0, 1}-lifted Gram matrix of the trace form (x, y) -> Tr(a x y) of the field with 2^n elements (an equivalent form of the Galois-ring bases of Klappenecker-Rötteler, Theorem 3), through the mod-4 identity Q(x + y) = Q(x) + Q(y) + 2 x^T S y and the nondegeneracy of the trace form; so IsMaxMUBCount (p^k) (p^k + 1) for every prime power, HasCompleteMUBs d iff IsMaxMUBCount d (d + 1) for d >= 2, and the values 3, 5, 9 in dimensions 2, 4, 8 also by explicit kernel-checked tables. Weiner's gap (Weiner 2013, Corollary 3.4): any d mutually unbiased bases of C^d extend, by one more basis, to a complete set of d + 1, the given bases keeping their places, for every d (and in the existence form, HasMUBs d d implies HasCompleteMUBs d), by Weiner's proof with its operator-algebra steps written out. The orthogonal projection Phi onto the matrices with a constant diagonal in every one of the d bases has a Kraus form X -> sum_i K_i^* X K_i whose operators K_i have constant diagonals themselves (Weiner's Lemma 3.2, through his Lemma 2.1, sum_k A_k^* X A_k = Tr(X) 1 for an orthonormal basis A_k of the matrix space, recalled there from Werner 2001); at a fixed point X the Kadison-Schwarz defect sum_i K_i^* X^* X K_i - Phi(X)^* Phi(X) is the sum of the squares (X K_i - K_i X)^* (X K_i - K_i X) and has zero trace, so the K_i commute with one another and with their adjoints (in place of the Schwarz inequality and the multiplicative-domain theorem of Choi 1974 that the paper's Lemma 3.1 uses); and the rank-one projectors of a common eigenbasis of the K_i are fixed by Phi, hence have constant diagonals, hence are unbiased to every basis of the family. Corollaries: k >= d bases give a complete set; for d >= 2, d is never the maximal number (in particular mu(6) != 6), and the maximal number is d + 1 or below d. The maximal number mu(d): two bases in every dimension; HasMUBs (p^k) m iff m <= p^k + 1; mu(d) is unique, exists for d >= 2 and lies in [3, d + 1], and does not exist for d = 1; formal-conjectures' mutuallyUnbiasedBases_dim6_bounds, 3 <= mu(6) <= 7, left with sorry there. Reconstruction (Scott 2006, eq. (9)): a complete set of d + 1 bases determines every matrix, X = sum_{s,l} Tr(X P_{s,l}) P_{s,l} - Tr(X) 1 with P_{s,l} the projector onto column l of basis s (after Ivanović 1981 and Wootters-Fields 1989), and so does a SIC family, X = sum_i ((d + 1) Tr(X P_i) - Tr X)/d P_i (its projectors are linearly independent, Renes-Blume-Kohout-Scott-Caves 2004, section II). Second moments (Klappenecker-Rötteler 2005, Theorems 3 and 5; Renes-Blume-Kohout-Scott-Caves 2004, p. 4; Scott 2006, eq. (8)): for all matrices X, Y, sum_{s,l} Tr(X P_{s,l}) Tr(Y P_{s,l}) = Tr(XY) + Tr X Tr Y for a complete set and (d + 1) sum_i Tr(X P_i) Tr(Y P_i) = d (Tr(XY) + Tr X Tr Y) for a SIC family; hence the data Tr(X P_{s,l}), and the SIC-POVM outcomes Tr(X P_i)/d with the factor d(d + 1), give ||X||_HS^2 + |Tr X|^2, the Hilbert-Schmidt distance of two matrices with equal traces, and the purity Tr(rho^2) of a Hermitian rho with Tr rho = 1 (Larsen 1990, not read, as stated by Wu-Yu-Mølmer 2009; Scott 2006, eqs. (32), (36), (55)). A SIC family in C^d is d^2 unit vectors with pairwise squared overlap 1/(d + 1); HasSICPOVM d says one exists. Theorems: N unit vectors of C^d with one squared overlap c != 1 on every pair satisfy N <= d^2 (the absolute bound of Delsarte-Goethals-Seidel 1975, the complex form of Gerzon's bound; the rank-one projectors are linearly independent), and with c = 1 the family may be any length; for d >= 2, d^2 such vectors have c = 1/(d + 1) and resolve the identity, sum_i (1/d) |phi_i><phi_i| = 1, so every SIC family is a POVM (Renes-Blume-Kohout-Scott-Caves 2004), HasSICPOVM d holds iff C^d has d^2 equiangular unit vectors, and a family at the SIC angle has at most d^2 members; Welch's bound (Welch 1974, the bound for k = 1, in the frame-potential form of Benedetto-Fickus 2003): N unit vectors of C^d have sum_{i,j} |<phi_i, phi_j>|^2 >= N^2/d, by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for the identity and the frame operator in the matrix space; hence N >= 2 unit vectors with one squared overlap c on every pair have c >= (N - d)/(d (N - 1)), pairwise squared overlaps at most alpha with alpha d < 1 give N (1 - alpha d) <= d (1 - alpha) (the relative bound), and at most d^2 unit vectors have every pairwise squared overlap at most 1/(d + 1). Welch's equality case (Mixon-Needham-Shonkwiler-Villar, Proposition 1 and its proof): sum_{i,j} |<phi_i, phi_j>|^2 - N^2/d = ||S - (N/d) 1||_HS^2 for the frame operator S = sum_i |phi_i><phi_i|, so equality holds exactly for a tight frame; at equality in the relative bound every pairwise squared overlap is alpha and S = (N/d) 1 (Strohmer-Heath 2003, Theorem 2.3); d^2 unit vectors with every pairwise squared overlap at most 1/(d + 1) are a SIC family, and HasSICPOVM d holds iff such vectors exist; and pairwise squared overlaps at most 1/(d + 1) + epsilon give ||S/d - 1||_HS^2 <= (d^2 - 1) epsilon for d >= 1, a bound on the resolution of the identity only. SIC-POVMs exist in dimensions 2 (the tetrahedron), 3 (the Hesse configuration), 4 (the sixteen Weyl-Heisenberg translates of Appleby's exact fiducial, Appleby 2005, eq. (149), credited there to Zauner and to Renes et al.; covariance reduces the 240 overlaps to fifteen, proved by exact trigonometric and radical identities in cos(pi/8), sin(pi/8) and sqrt(2 + sqrt 5)) and 8 (Hoggar's 64 lines: the orbit of (-1 + 2i, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1)/sqrt 12 under the three-qubit Pauli group, Jedwab-Wiebe 2015, Example 4, checked by the kernel over all ordered pairs). Sixty compared statements, kernel-only. As of 2026-10-10 no formalization of the general bound, of the prime-power constructions, of the factorization corollary, of the complex absolute bound with its equality case, of Weiner's gap for general d, of Welch's bound, of the two reconstruction formulas for every matrix or of a SIC-POVM in dimension 4 was located in the Palomar registry, Mathlib, formal-conjectures, openai/math, physlib, the other Lean repositories searched, the Isabelle AFP, the Rocq package index or arXiv; none of the second moment of a SIC family with its norm, distance and purity forms, of Welch's deficit with its equality case, of the equality case of the relative bound, of the SIC family from d^2 vectors at or below the SIC angle or of the frame-defect bound was located in the Palomar registry, Mathlib, formal-conjectures, openai/math, physlib or the-omega-institute/trureturing. Read 2026-10-14, after that search: marozols/SIC-existence (public 2026-10-09, Lean v4.34.1, self-assessed, unregistered) states SICs in every dimension and, in RSIC.lean, the N = d^2 equality case, in its own vocabulary, so a dimension-4 SIC and that equality case exist elsewhere in Lean; the statements here are over formal-conjectures' definitions and were proved independently. The neighbours: the dimension-2 MUB case is formal-conjectures' mutuallyUnbiasedBases_dim2; the dimension-6 projector bound and the Kronecker lemma are in the XC0R fork of formal-conjectures (adapted here, see NOTICE); the dimension-2 and 3 SIC overlaps are in zblore/csd-lean4; the-omega-institute/trureturing kernel-checks the same 64 Hoggar vectors and the Hesse SIC in its own vocabulary, proves that the trace pairings with a complete family of rank-one contexts determine every matrix, proves the density-matrix formula under an assumed completeness hypothesis, and proves the second moment of a complete set in operator form with the purity identity for density matrices (complete_context_collision_conservation, 2026-08-28); openai/math holds mu(6) <= 5 and Weiner's gap at d = 6 (six_extend_to_seven), with lemmas for general n (commutator_trace_identity, commute_of_kraus_fixed, exists_joint_projection_basis) that make the same elementary move as the route here, the Schwarz defect of a Kraus map as a sum of squared commutators; the Kadison-Schwarz inequality for Kraus and completely positive maps is in physlib, QuAIR/Lean-QIT and kencyke/quantum-system. Not claimed: anything about dimension 6 beyond 3 <= mu(6) <= 7 and mu(6) != 6 (openai/math holds mu(6) <= 5), SICs in dimensions 5 to 7, that a family near the SIC angle is close to a SIC family, any first formalization.
title: Finite quantum designs: mutually unbiased bases, SIC-POVMs, and the Welch and Gerzon bounds

abstract: A Lean 4 and Mathlib formalization of Theorems A and B of arXiv:2609.35632 on the central configurations of the planar Newtonian four-body problem. For every choice of four positive masses and every cyclic order of the bodies there is exactly one strictly convex central configuration with that cyclic order, up to similarity, so there are exactly three convex central configurations up to similarity. This answers Problem 10 in the list of Albouy, Cabral and Santos (2012). The main step of the paper is Theorem B: at every strictly convex central configuration of positive masses, the Hessian form Q of U + (λ/2)I is at least one quarter of its radial part K. It follows that every convex central configuration is a nondegenerate local minimum of U I^(1/2), whose Hessian vanishes exactly on the tangent space of the orbit of the similarities. The computer-assisted step, a branch and bound with interval arithmetic over the three-dimensional set of normalized convex central configurations in the coordinates of Corbera, Cors and Roberts, proves tr S < 3/4 and is checked by Lean's kernel with `decide +kernel` in 7307 certificate theorems. No compiled code is trusted, and the proofs use only Lean's three standard axioms.
title: Uniqueness of four-body convex central configurations for all masses

abstract: A Lean 4 and Mathlib proof that at least one of the eight values ζ(7), ζ(9), ζ(11), ζ(13), ζ(15), ζ(17), ζ(19), ζ(21) of the Riemann zeta function is irrational. The statement uses only Mathlib's riemannZeta, the theorem has no hypotheses, and its proof uses only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. The shortest list of odd zeta values starting at ζ(7) that our literature search found proved to contain an irrational number was ζ(7), ζ(9), …, ζ(35) (W. Zudilin, Math. Notes 2001). The proof uses the very-well-poised linear forms of Zudilin (J. Théor. Nombres Bordeaux 2004, §8) with five derivatives, 23 factors and the direction vector η₀ = 160, η = (47, 47, 47, 47, 48, 50, 50, 51, 52, …, 66); they are linear forms in 1, ζ(7), ζ(9), …, ζ(21) with rational coefficients. Zudilin anticipated such an improvement but could not prove the asymptotics of his forms (his Lemma 20) for more than three derivatives. The proof here does not need them. The denominators of the coefficients are bounded by Zudilin's arithmetic lemma, the prime number theorem (proved from a vendored Lean proof of the Wiener–Ikehara theorem) and a kernel-checked table of 2602 pieces of Zudilin's function φ. For large n the forms are bounded by e^(−748.1n), through a contour integral on a fixed vertical line, pointwise estimates and certified numerical inequalities, without saddle-point analysis. They are non-zero if the eight values are rational, because at the auxiliary primes ℓ = 63n − 1, of which there are infinitely many by Dirichlet's theorem, the constant term has ℓ-adic valuation −5 while the coefficients of the zeta values are ℓ-integral. The theorem does not say which value is irrational. The mathematics and the Lean code were produced by AI agents under human direction and have not been refereed.
title: At least one of ζ(7), ζ(9), …, ζ(21) is irrational

abstract: Lean 4 results (core Lean, no dependencies, no axioms beyond the standard three) about law 1518 of the Equational Theories Project, x = (y ◇ y) ◇ (x ◇ (y ◇ x)). Theorem A: in every magma satisfying 1518 and 3862 (x ◇ x = (x ◇ (x ◇ x)) ◇ x), writing S x = x ◇ x, the set {x, S x, S (S x)} is closed under ◇ with u ◇ v = S v and S (S (S x)) = x; hence every one-generated such magma is the trivial magma or the three-element cyclic shift x ◇ y = y + 1. This proves a classification conjectured by Terence Tao on the Lean Zulip on 2024-11-29 (message 485148288). That message assumed 1518 together with all four of 47, 614, 817 and 3862 and carried no finiteness hypothesis; assuming 3862 alone is no weaker, because Matthew Bolan reported the same day (message 485153888) that 1518 and 3862 already imply the other three. What is added here is a machine-checked proof, not a weaker hypothesis: no proof of the classification was found in the venues searched. Theorem A is what the compared declarations state. Outside them the repository holds an explicit family of finite 1518-magmas that do violate the four targets, with two members checked by kernel evaluation, and kernel-checked certificate identities behind a cohomological obstruction theorem (every 1518-cocycle over the shift with finite fibre is a coboundary), whose reduction is a written proof, and the computations classifying base-dependent extensions of the shift.
title: One-generated (1518 + 3862)-magmas are trivial or the Z/3 shift; an explicit family of finite 1518-magmas violating laws 47, 614, 817, 3862

abstract: Formalization in Lean 4 / mathlib of the existing paper by Furber, Mardare, Panangaden, and Scott, Interpreting Lambda Calculus in Domain-Valued Random Variables (LIPIcs, Vol. 363, CSL 2026, Article 48). This repository formalizes that published mathematics; it does not present the paper's results as new mathematics originating in this repository. Three capstones sit on top of the rest of the paper: Theorem 26 (internal λ-interpretation in SetoidF_A), Corollary 34 (the Engeler model with numerals in V^A), and Theorem 43 (two fair-coin subsets of ℕ that are incomparable under the λ-definable many-one preorder). Full Corollary 34 remains kernel-checked in the library and is not represented by a weaker Mathlib-only proxy. Lean is written by AI agents under the direction and review of the author. abstract: Glauberman and Norton (Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 119, 1993) end their paper on a combinatorial problem that arises in the proof of the Feit–Thompson odd order theorem with a question of Péterfalvi: can the hypothesis of their Proposition 9 be satisfied for p = 3? The same question is Problem 1 in Appendix C of Bender and Glauberman, Local Analysis for the Odd Order Theorem (1994). Let F be the field with p^q elements, P its additive group, U its group of units of norm one over the prime field, H the semidirect product P ⋊ U, and P₀ the image of the additive group of the prime field in H. Hypothesis (B) asks for an injective homomorphism σ from H into a group G, a finite abelian subgroup Q of G whose order is prime to p, and an element y of Q, such that σ(P₀) normalizes Q and σ(P₀)^y normalizes σ(U). Proposition 9 also assumes condition (A): q does not divide p − 1. This project proves in Lean 4 that the answer is negative: for every prime q with q ∤ 3 − 1, no group G, finite or infinite, satisfies hypothesis (B) with p = 3. It also proves Péterfalvi's example from the same paper, which shows that SL(2, 2^q) satisfies hypothesis (B) with p = 2, so the hypothesis is not empty. The proof is new. It turns a witness of hypothesis (B) into relations between three copies of the additive group of the field with 3^q elements, and it rules out these relations by arithmetic in that field.
title: Péterfalvi's Problem for p = 3: No Group Satisfies Hypothesis (B)

abstract: A Lean 4 and Mathlib proof that at least one of the 2-adic zeta values ζ₂(7), ζ₂(9) is irrational. The theorem has no hypotheses, and its proof uses only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. The values are defined through the Volkenborn integral: zeta2 s = J(s−1)/((s−1)·2^s), where J(s) is the 2-adic limit of the Riemann sums 2^(−N) Σ_{x<2^N} (x+1/2)^(−s), and the theorem also proves that these limits exist. By Lemma 2.8 of Lai, Sprang and Zudilin (IMRN 2026), zeta2 s is the Kubota–Leopoldt value ζ₂(s) = L₂(s, ω^(1−s)) for s ≥ 2. That identification is cited, not formalised; it only involves a non-zero rational factor, which does not affect irrationality. The result sharpens Theorem 1.1 (case s = 3) of L. Lai (Int. J. Number Theory 2025), which shows that at least one of ζ₂(7), ζ₂(9), ζ₂(11), ζ₂(13) is irrational, and it implies the companion result, formalised in a separate repository, that at least one of ζ₂(7), ζ₂(9), ζ₂(11) is irrational. The proof uses linear forms S_n = ∫ R_n'''(t+1/2) dt in 1, ζ₂(7), ζ₂(9) built from the shifted well-poised rational functions R_n(t) = (2t+n) Π_{m=1}^{6} (t+1/2−h_m)_(n+2h_m) / (t)_(n+1)^6 with h = (n/40)(−17, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6). The 2-adic size of S_n comes from Lai's and Sprang's Δ-calculus. The size of the coefficients comes from a contour-integral representation and a saddle-point bound, whose numerical inequalities are certified in Lean. The odd part of the denominators is bounded by Legendre-type counts at the poles, the vanishing of R_n at half-integers, kernel-checked certificates and the prime number theorem (proved here from a vendored Lean proof of the Wiener–Ikehara theorem). If both values were rational, the valuations of the coefficients at the prime n − 1 (an idea of Lai and Sprang) would make S_n non-zero for infinitely many n, and Lai's irrationality criterion gives the contradiction. The mathematics and the Lean code were produced by AI agents under human direction and have not been refereed.
title: At least one of the 2-adic zeta values ζ₂(7), ζ₂(9) is irrational

abstract: A complete Lean 4 / Mathlib proof that the 7-adic zeta value ζ₇(3) is irrational. Here ζ₇(3) = L₇(3, ω⁻²) is the Kubota–Leopoldt value, equal to the 7-adic limit of the Euler-corrected Bernoulli numbers −(1 − 7^{w−1}) B_w / w over the weights w = 6·7^{n+1} − 2. The same is proved for η = ζ₇(3)/2. The proof is a determinant irrationality argument on the modular curve X₀(7), in four parts: independence of seven explicit germs attached to the weight −2 seven-adic Eisenstein series, with a uniform zero estimate; a seven-adic annular saving; an auxiliary-prime denominator estimate; and an Archimedean energy estimate with a kernel-checked numerical margin. It also uses an internal proof of the geometric continuation of the target series to every radius below 49, via a twisted U₇ matrix bound and initial overconvergence obtained from classical Eisenstein approximants. The Lean endpoints depend only on propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. The mathematical argument has not been refereed. The work is human-directed, with extensive AI assistance in both the mathematics and the Lean development; see the automation section and PROVENANCE.md.
title: Irrationality of the 7-adic zeta value ζ₇(3)

abstract: A Lean 4 classification of the number of good partitions of an initial interval, where a good partition of {1, ..., n} is a set of pairwise disjoint nonempty blocks of at most three integers covering {1, ..., n}, each block summing to a power of three, and count n is the number of them. With N_u = {1, 2, 3, 4} union {3^t - 4, 3^t - 2, 3^t - 1, 3^t, 3^t + 1, 3^t + 2, 3^t + 3, 3^t + 5 : t >= 2} and E_2 = {13} union {3^t - 3 : t >= 2} union {3^t - 6 : t >= 3}, the four compared theorems say that for n >= 1 the count is 1 exactly on N_u, is 2 exactly on E_2, and is at least 3 elsewhere, and that the count is 2 at every 3^t - 6 with t >= 3. The source proves uniqueness for every n in N_u, records exactly two partitions at 3^t - 3 and at 13, and conjectures, immediately after that theorem, more than two at every other n, reporting a computer check up to n = 844; the family 3^t - 6 (first member 21) refutes that conjecture as printed, and the converse of the uniqueness statement is proved here. The lower bounds are three explicit partitions transported by four constructions each of which keeps a recoverable component; the exact values are exhaustive enumerations at twenty values n <= 86, kernel-checked and complete by a theorem about the search, carried to every power of three by stabilization above a threshold.
title: gnm-lean: the number of partitions of {1, ..., n} into sets of at most three elements with power-of-three sums

abstract: Formalizes finite strategic-form games with player-specific finite move sets, pure profiles, unilateral deviations, best responses, dominant strategies, and two distinct potential notions. Pure Nash equilibrium is defined over utility preorders by the absence of a strict improvement; weak-inequality characterizations are restricted to linear orders. The library names the one-way improvement condition a generalized ordinal potential and reserves ordinal potential for the standard bidirectional strict-sign condition. It proves a global potential-maximizer certificate for pure Nash equilibrium, the standard Nash/local-potential-maximum equivalence, and acyclicity of the better-response relation for the generalized class. The development also gives checked counterexamples and Prisoner's-Dilemma/coordination/matching-pennies/rock-paper-scissors examples. Its native mixed layer proves support equalization, Dirac transport, the normalized excess-map reduction, and the closed/compact/ convex/continuous finite mixed-profile geometry. It also proves general finite mixed-Nash existence on a common nonempty move type by connecting the native excess map to an attributed, kernel-checked product-of-simplices Brouwer theorem. This is a reusable formalization artifact, not a claim of new mathematics or the first Lean proof of Nash existence.
title: Native Lean finite Nash equilibria

abstract:
Erdős Problem 647 asks whether there is any n > 24 with max_{m < n} (m + tau(m)) <= n + 2, where tau counts divisors. The value n = 24 satisfies it and the question is open. This entry certifies a bounded exclusion: no such n exists in (24, 10^8]. It does not resolve the problem and asserts nothing about n > 10^8.
The exclusion is certified rather than searched at check time. A witness at a cover position is an offset together with prime-power pairs dividing m, certifying tau(m) >= prod (e + 1); every prime in a pair is below 1024 and is checked prime by eleven trial divisions, so no primality certificates appear anywhere. A chain of witnesses covers the interval and each certificate chunk is discharged by a single decide against the chain checker, so the Lean kernel certifies the arithmetic and the generator that produced it is never trusted.
The audience is the community working on the Erdős problems database and its Lean formalizations, for whom a machine-checked lower bound on the search range is directly usable, and researchers building certificate-based exclusions in elementary number theory, for whom the witness format and its kernel-evaluable checkers are the transferable part.
title: A kernel-checked exclusion certificate for Erdős Problem 647, to 10^8

abstract: A kernel-checked Lean formalization of the exact no-broken-circuit volume identity for hard-sphere Mayer cluster integrals and the stronger dimension-three fork-packing upper bound for each tree-owned NBC region. The development proves finite broken-circuit cancellation, the measurable finite-region decomposition, the anchored Euclidean product-measure theorem, and its explicit flat-coordinate transport.  Its geometric result is the attachment-aware estimate Vol(NBC_T) <= (17/32)^hardSphereNu T * hardSphereKappa^(k-1), where hardSphereNu T is the maximum cardinality of a packing of pairwise vertex-disjoint, order-compatible forks in T.  A formal fork is an ordered triple (a,b,c) with a < b < c, center a, leaves b,c, and tree edges {a,b} and {a,c}.  The central contribution is the complete pointwise-to-integral bridge together with the orientation-aware measure-preserving factorization that realizes the per-fork volume suppression.

abstract: Kernel-checked Salem's theorem — every Pisot number is a limit point of Salem numbers from both sides (R. Salem, Algebraic Numbers and Fourier Analysis, D. C. Heath, 1963, Ch. III, Theorem IV, p. 30; origin R. Salem, Duke Math. J. 12 (1945)) — with both of Salem's constructions, each stated as a construction. Three compared statements carry the surface. (1) salem_theorem — the theorem for Pisot numbers: a real algebraic integer alpha > 1 every other complex root of whose minimal polynomial has modulus < 1 (spelled as 1 < alpha, IsIntegral Z alpha, and every z in (minpoly Q alpha).aroots C other than alpha has norm < 1 — the spelling of the Pisot predicate in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures, inlined) has, for every eps > 0, a Salem number in (alpha - eps, alpha) and one in (alpha, alpha + eps). (2) salem_construction_two_sided — Salem's main construction z^m P(z) ± z^p P(1/z) with its family root in the conclusion: for the pattern data of a monic integer polynomial P (one real root alpha > 1, every other complex root strictly inside the unit circle, conjugation-closed) under the nondegeneracy P(1/alpha) != 0 — a proviso that on the pattern domain is strictly STRONGER than Boyd's — coinciding, when P is the minimal polynomial, with Boyd's "provided P is not a reciprocal quadratic" (Math. Comp. 32 (1978), p. 1252, eq. (26)) and with the reason clause of Salem's, "so that Q and P will not be identical" (Salem's stated hypothesis, "theta not a quadratic unit", is stronger; fidelity (g)) — there is a sign e = ±1, the sign of P(1/alpha), such that for every eps > 0 some X^m P + e P.reverse with m >= 2 has a Salem root in (alpha - eps, alpha) and some X^m P - e P.reverse with m >= 2 has a Salem root in (alpha, alpha + eps); P.reverse is z^p P(1/z), p = deg P. (3) salem_quadratic_unit — the excluded case, Salem's second construction (1963, p. 31) with its family root in the conclusion: for the reciprocal quadratic Pisot units alpha^2 = r alpha - 1, r >= 3 an integer, and every eps > 0, some (X^2 - rX + 1)(X^{2m} + 1) + X^{m+1} with m >= 1 has a Salem root in (alpha - eps, alpha) and some (X^2 - rX + 1)(X^{2m} + 1) - X^{m+1} with m >= 1 has a Salem root in (alpha, alpha + eps) — the Chebyshev family (x - r) T_m(x) ∓ 1 pulled back through x = y + 1/y. Statement (1) is the theorem; (2) and (3) each carry their construction and neither follows from (1), their conclusions naming a root of a specific polynomial; Boyd's "for all sufficiently large m" is NOT stated — (2) and (3) assert, per eps, the existence of some index m. A Salem number is spelled by Salem's definition of the class T (1963, p. 26): a real algebraic integer tau > 1 all of whose other conjugates lie in the closed unit disk, at least one on the unit circle — with the clause that 1/tau is a conjugate stated explicitly. Classically that clause and "degree at least 4" are consequences (Salem 1963, p. 26; Smyth 2015, Lemma 1); the equivalence is NOT formalized here, and the formal predicate is the stronger conjunction, which is the CONCLUSION of every compared statement — nothing is assumed of it. THE ROUTE: (1) is transported from a pattern-form theorem in the proof modules (salem_theorem_full), stated for any monic integer polynomial with the pattern data — a larger index set than the Pisot numbers (X^k times a minimal polynomial has the pattern) but equivalent in content, since the large root of any pattern polynomial is itself a Pisot number — through the bridge that the minimal polynomial over Z of a Pisot number carries the pattern data (the Gauss step: the minimal polynomial over Q is the rational image of the one over Z, since Z is integrally closed; separability of the irreducible minimal polynomial in characteristic zero; conjugation-invariance of integer coefficients). The pattern-form theorem splits on P(1/alpha) = 0: the nonzero branch is the assembly PdtSalemEndgame.salem_two_sided; the zero branch reduces to PdtSalemQuadUnit.salem_two_sided_quad_unit by a supporting lemma (reciprocal_quadratic_of_inv_root: a pattern polynomial vanishing at 1/alpha forces alpha^2 = r alpha - 1 with r >= 3 — the elementary "reciprocal Pisot implies quadratic", McKee–Smyth 2012, Lemma 6.2). Those two assemblies discard the index and the family; (2) and (3) are the same assemblies re-run in the bridge module SalemPisot with both kept. The book runs Case 1 under the proviso and handles the quadratic units in Case 2; the kernel unifies both cases in a single statement with no nondegeneracy hypothesis — a presentational unification of Salem's own two cases, not a mathematical strengthening of the theorem, which has no gap. The proofs use no argument principle and no Rouché theorem: the circle counts (m + p - 2 unimodular roots for the plus family z^m P + z^p P(1/z) with p = deg P, m + p - 3 plus the root z = 1 for the minus family, 2m for the quadratic-unit family) are intermediate-value arguments on explicit real phases; the trichotomy (every root unimodular or in {tau, 1/tau}) is a multiset squeeze against the degree; Salem-ness is an arithmetic certificate (the minimal polynomial divides the family; the Gauss step excludes degrees 1 and 2 and forces 1/tau a conjugate), with the integer degeneracies tau in Z and tau + 1/tau in Z discharged by finiteness along the ladders, or directly for the quadratic-unit family. NOT formalized: the equivalence of the Salem-number definitions (above); Boyd's converse (Boyd 1977: every Salem number arises from the construction); Salem 1944 (the Pisot numbers form a closed set); any rate of approach; Boyd's "for all sufficiently large m". As of the 2026-09-01 sweep (Mathlib at the pin and at master, Loogle, the Isabelle AFP at title/abstract/filename level, Coq, HOL Light, Metamath, arXiv; GitHub native code search and Mizar not run) the entry is not aware of a prior formalization of Salem's theorem or of Salem numbers in any surveyed prover ecosystem; the one adjacent hit is the IsPisot definition in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures (the definition and the golden-ratio instance; no Salem numbers), whose spelling the compared statement adopts. abstract: Formalizes the binary Grushko--Neumann theorem: the minimal number of generators of a free product of two finitely generated groups is the sum of the minimal numbers of generators of the factors. The central theorem is proved by a kernel-checked finite labelled-graph reduction. For a minimal null path, the implemented reduction uniformly performs a source unfold, a subsequent safe fold, and an explicit monochromatic-vertex contraction; this gives the strict decrease used by strong induction and the separated-generator lower bound. The repository also retains the finite-core and free-group rank lemmas from the surrounding development as reusable supporting infrastructure, but only the global Grushko theorem declaration is selected by the public Challenge and Comparator.

abstract: Kernel-checked general-n theorems for the golden family — the ladder of trinomials x^n - x - 1, whose unique real root r_n > 1 descends from the golden ratio (n = 2) through the plastic number (n = 3) toward 1. The family's structural boundary falls at n = 3; this entry proves the morphic half unconditionally at general n and holds the Pisot half as the measure⟺Pisot equivalence, the unconditional n = 4 non-Pisot statement, and the Siegel-conditional strict excess for n >= 4, from the family's own arithmetic, with no per-degree case check above the boundary. Eleven compared statements carry the surface. (1) The root ladder: for every n >= 2 the root exists, is unique above 1, and strictly decreases in n. (2) The morphic boundary, UNCONDITIONAL: r_n satisfies the golden ratio's two scale closures p + 1 = p^k and p - 1 = p^(-l) (Aarts-Fokkink-Kruijtzer 2001, spelled inline) if and only if n <= 3 — the classification pins morphic numbers to the golden ratio and the plastic number, and descent puts r_n below 1.23, hence below both, for n >= 4. (3) Circle exclusion: x^n - x - 1 has no complex root of modulus 1, for any n (|z| = |z + 1| = 1 forces z^2 + z + 1 = 0, so z^3 = 1, and every residue of n mod 3 is impossible). (4) The Jensen lower bound r_n <= M(x^n - x - 1), by the monic root-product form of the Mahler measure. (5) The equivalence M(x^n - x - 1) = r_n iff every other complex root lies strictly inside the unit circle — the honest form of "the family's Mahler-measure boundary IS its Pisot boundary": the equivalence is itself the kernel theorem (exact because the family never has unimodular roots, and its trinomials are separable by Selmer irreducibility), stated once and never counted as a pair of separate boundaries. (6) The Siegel-conditional closure: IF the plastic number is the smallest Pisot number — Siegel 1944, entering ONLY as an explicit named hypothesis, with "Pisot" unfolded in the statement — THEN r_n < M(x^n - x - 1) for every n >= 4. Siegel's minimality is the single classical input anywhere in the entry; every other statement is kernel-checked unconditionally, and Siegel's theorem itself is not proved here. (7) Q < psi: the quartic root (q^4 = q + 1) lies strictly below psi (psi^4 = psi^3 + 1), the Mahler measure of the n = 4 member. (8) THE SHARED LEMMA, at general n: no root of x^n - x - 1 satisfies z^2 + z + 1 = 0 (z^3 = 1 and every residue of n mod 3 is impossible). It supplies the obstruction in the circle exclusion (3), which is re-derived from it as an explicit corollary (the circle geometry supplies the reduction), and up to the substitution z^n = z + 1 (under which z^n + z^2 = 0 iff z^2 + z + 1 = 0) it is Mathlib's public Polynomial.X_pow_sub_X_sub_one_irreducible_aux — the first step of Mathlib's Selmer proof, hence of the morphic classification behind (2) — restated in the family's own vocabulary; compared as the named shared core, not as new mathematics. (9) Witness b_3 (b^3 = b^2 + 1): every other complex root of x^3 = x^2 + 1 has modulus < 1, and b_3 is not morphic. (10) Witness psi (psi^4 = psi^3 + 1): every other complex root of x^4 = x^3 + 1 has modulus < 1, and psi is not morphic. (11) The golden quartic root is NOT Pisot: for q^4 = q + 1, some complex root of x^4 = x + 1 other than q has modulus > 1 (every nonreal root does — quartic_conj_norm_gt_one in the proof module, not compared) — with (10) and (7) the degree-4 separation: Q and psi are both algebraic units with constant term of modulus one (unit-ness is elementary and not compared: Q^-1 = Q^3 - 1, psi^-1 = psi^3 - psi^2), yet Q is not Pisot and psi is, so the unit condition alone does not locate the Pisot boundary. (10) and (11) are not independent evidence: x^4 - x^3 - 1 is the image of x^4 - x - 1 under x -> -1/x, so the Pisot half of (10) says x^4 - x - 1 has one root inside the unit circle and three outside, and (11) follows; they are compared separately for the two families' sakes. THE STORY: one shared lemma beneath both boundaries (naming the family-specific arithmetic core, not the whole proof graph: (2) and (6) also share the elementary descent r_n < 1.23 < rho, and the kernel-held Pisot side is localized by Siegel plus descent, the angle route being context); the boundaries localize by different routes — an angle for Pisot (the escape arc between the primitive cube roots of unity, giving the outside-root count 1 + 2*floor((2n - 1)/6), Howell-Kyle 2018 Theorem 3 via the reciprocal trinomial; context, NOT formalized), a degree for morphic (the cofactor x^2 - x + 1 forcing k = 3; formalized) — and the classes are in fact separable: (9)-(11) hold the witnesses and the degree-4 separation in the kernel, with no Siegel input, showing the classes coming apart inside the sister trinomial family itself (Pisot units below phi that are not morphic). The entry never claims the two boundaries are independent (they share the lemma) and never claims a common cause for their location. Two spellings of "Pisot" appear: the trinomial-roots form of (5), (9), (10), (11) and the minimal-polynomial form of the siegel hypothesis; they coincide exactly when the defining trinomial is irreducible (Selmer for (5), (11); x^3 - x^2 - 1 and x^4 - x^3 - 1 have no rational root and no integer quadratic factorization, for (9), (10)). On the sister family x^m - x^(m-1) - 1 the classes come apart: b_2 = phi and b_5 = rho exactly, so morphic only for m = 2, 5 (AFK, kernel-held, plus strict decrease); Pisot at m = 2, 5 is elementary, though at m = 5 the quintic is reducible with two roots ON the unit circle, so b_5 is Pisot in the minimal-polynomial sense only; the m = 3, 4 members are the kernel-held witnesses; not Pisot for 6 <= m <= 30 numerically and for all m >= 6 Siegel-conditionally (b_6 < rho). The n <= 4 instances of this boundary are registered content of the author's sibling entries (PALOMAR-2026-08-31-000004, PALOMAR-2026-09-01-000005, and PALOMAR-2026-09-01-000008) and are cited as context imports, never re-compared. The classical route to the n >= 4 strict excess (Smyth 1971), the limit behavior of the family measures (Lawton 1983, Smyth 1981, Verger-Gaugry 2016, Stankov 2014), and the outside-root count (Howell-Kyle 2018, with Brilleslyper-Schaubroeck 2014 for the unimodular criterion and Stankov 2014 for the asymptotic density) are cited context, not formalized — see the labeled context block in the sources. As of the 2026-09-01 sweep the entry is not aware of a prior formalization of the general-n family boundary, of Siegel minimality, of Smyth's nonreciprocal bound, or of Pisot-number theory in any surveyed prover ecosystem; Mathlib supplies Selmer irreducibility and the Mahler-measure development as infrastructure.
